rationale: B wins because it is more disciplined about proof: it turns the launch into testable reporter questions instead of declaring the market result. A has one of the best raw angles in "Why a major SaaS company is shipping offline mode in 2026," but it also asserts "Notion's compliance stack puts Confluence and SharePoint on the defensive" before the facts earn that fight. B's "Get the proof first — a named bank, or a specific compliance/audit confirmation" is the grown-up move here.
gaps_in_A: "anchored in named institutions" is wrong as written. The update says four of the five largest US banks are piloting, but gives no named banks.
"Notion's compliance stack puts Confluence and SharePoint on the defensive" names threatened competitors the update never supplied and turns a hypothesis into a headline.
"US cloud platforms forced to localize data" overstates causality. The update says Notion added EU and Australia residency options; it does not prove regulatory force or a documented market pattern.

"pilot-eligible" to "procurement-approvable" overclaims the bank evidence. Pilots are not procurement approval, and A knows it because its own proof section asks whether they are paid or evaluation-stage.
gaps_in_B: "quietly testing" adds color the facts do not support. A pilot is not automatically quiet.

B leaves a real angle on the floor: it refuses "Notion ships offline-first editing" but never rebuilds it into the sharper story A saw, namely why a cloud SaaS company is shipping offline mode in 2026.
"historically seen as too lightweight for their compliance bar" is plausible, but it is still an inference. Label it as a skepticism to test, not a fact.
The data-residency angle is a little soft at the headline level: "keep their data at home" sounds friendly, but the story lives or dies on exactly what residency covers.
